क्या चुनाव आयोग की विश्वसनीयता पर सवाल उठाना लोकतंत्र को कमजोर करने की कोशिश है? या फिर संवैधानिक संस्थाओं से जवाबदेही मांगना विपक्ष का अधिकार है?

भारत का चुनाव आयोग देश की सबसे महत्वपूर्ण संवैधानिक संस्थाओं में से एक है। लोकतंत्र की मजबूती काफी हद तक इस संस्था की निष्पक्षता, पारदर्शिता और विश्वसनीयता पर निर्भर करती है।

लेकिन आज भारतीय राजनीति में चुनाव आयोग लगातार राजनीतिक बहस के केंद्र में है। कांग्रेस और विपक्षी दलों द्वारा चुनाव आयोग की कार्यप्रणाली पर उठाए जा रहे सवालों ने एक नई बहस को जन्म दिया है।

क्या राजनीतिक आरोपों से संवैधानिक संस्थाओं की साख प्रभावित होती है? क्या बिना पर्याप्त प्रमाण के लगाए गए आरोप जनता के विश्वास को कमजोर कर सकते हैं? क्या विपक्ष की आलोचना लोकतांत्रिक जवाबदेही का हिस्सा है, या फिर इससे संस्थाओं की विश्वसनीयता पर असर पड़ता है?

इस वीडियो में समझिए चुनाव आयोग, कांग्रेस और भारतीय लोकतंत्र से जुड़ी दो महत्वपूर्ण राजनीतिक कहानियां। जानिए क्यों चुनाव आयोग की विश्वसनीयता आज भारतीय राजनीति का एक बड़ा मुद्दा बन चुकी है।

In today's episode, we sit down with Udit Chawla, co-founder of Wellwith, who took sea buckthorn, a little-known Himalayan berry India was barely using, and built a million-dollar brand.

We talk about how to find one underrated ingredient that can become a multi-million-dollar brand, and why creating your own category beats fighting giants in an existing market. He explains how a taxi driver in Ladakh, a PM Modi speech and unused patents in research institutes can lead you to your hero ingredient, and how to size any market in minutes using Amazon.

He reveals why he stayed off online marketplaces for two full years, sold juice for under 50 cents a glass outside a park, and how his first 100 customers wrote the ad copy that scaled his brand.

Kerala keeps falling for the same traps: Ponzi schemes, Telegram scams, weddings funded with borrowed money. Each time, we call it bad luck. What if it is really a decision-making problem?

Today on the Athishaktham Podcast (Episode 19), we have Dr. Vaisakhan Thampi, Assistant Professor of Physics at Mahatma Gandhi College, Thiruvananthapuram, whose talks bring science to Malayalis. This is not an episode about black holes. Sharique kept the usual science topics off the table to ask a bigger question: can the way a scientist works (the attitude, not the job title) help an ordinary person make better decisions about money, career, health and relationships?

The first half is about how humans think. What thinking actually is (do trees think?), how the human brain works and why it evolved to decide whether to move, not to analyse stocks, and what happens when a Stone Age brain lives in a digital world, from constant anxiety to the pot belly. Then how to think scientifically, in plain language: evidence, humility, objectivity and falsifiability.

Then it gets personal. The helmet you skip for a ride to the shop half a kilometre away. The ₹5 lakh someone close to you asks you to put into their business. The wedding a family borrows for and talks about with pride. The conversation names the cognitive bias behind each one, asks why smart people still make these mistakes, and turns the lens on finance content itself: why alarmist thumbnails beat careful explanations. At the end, Sharique asks what made him a scientific thinker in the first place. 🔥

What you'll learn in this episode:
- System 1 vs System 2: why fast thinking is cheap and slow thinking burns energy
- What falsifiability means?
- Is a debt trap really a money problem, or a thinking problem?
- Gambler's fallacy, confirmation bias, availability heuristic and the cashless effect, with Kerala examples
- The two parts of risk, and the one most people ignore
- Why we are "feeling machines that can think", and what that means for decision making
- Why people reject evidence even when it's right in front of them
- Lateral reading: how to check a viral message before you forward it

This looks like a science episode. It is really about decisions: the small daily ones that quietly compound into the life you end up with.

If you've been searching for how to take a decision, how to avoid mistakes, critical thinking, or the psychology of how the human mind works, explained in Malayalam, this is the long version.
